newsitem.title: USA: Coca-Cola earnings jump 38 percent; stock gains.
newsitem.headline: Coca-Cola earnings jump 38 percent; stock gains.

text.p: The Coca-Cola Co. Monday reported a 38 percent jump in first-quarter net income as unit sales growth exceeded Wall Street's expectations even in the huge but mature U.S. soft-drink market.
Coke's shares rose sharply on the New York Stock Exchange, even before the market corrected earlier losses and moved into the plus column. Coke rose $1.875 to close at $55.675.
The stock had fallen $3.25 Friday as the Dow headed into a 148-point tailspin.
The company said it earned $987 million, or 40 cents a share, on sales of $4.13 billion. In the first quarter a year earlier it earned $713 million, or 28 cents a share, on sales of $4.22 billion.
Earnings per share were boosted by an eight cent gain from the sale of Coke's 49 percent stake in Coca-Cola & Schweppes Beverages to Coca-Cola Enterprises Inc.

The results included an unexpectedly strong 9 percent gain in domestic unit sales volume, which represented Coke's best quarter in the United States in at least five years, according to analysts. In 1996, first-quarter unit sales volumes grew 8 percent in the U.S. market.
Analysts estimated that the pace of growth in U.S. unit sales boosted Coke's domestic market share to 43 percent, from 42 percent at the end of last year.

"Results like this in our flagship market, coupled with share gains, demonstrate again that our U.S. business is far from being a mature market for soft drinks -- in fact, it is capable of dramatic growth," Coke Chairman Roberto Goizueta said in a statement.

Worldwide unit case volume grew 9 percent while gallon shipments of concentrates and syrups increased 7 percent. Both exceeded company expectations of 7-8 percent and 5-6 percent growth, respectively.

"Our extremely strong first quarter unit case volume gain demonstrates the continuing power of our aligned global bottling system and is a solid start toward, once again, achieving our long term volume and EPS growth objectives in 1997," Goizueta added.
"We remain sharply focused on strengthening our system to capture the immense opportunities that exist around the world."

On Wall Street, Coke's admission that a strong dollar had led to some erosion in revenues prompted an equity analyst at Standard & Poor's Corp. to downgrade the stock to "hold" from "accumulate" on expectations that the dollar would move still higher in coming months.
The S&P analyst, Ken Shea, also reduced his 1997 earnings estimates to $1.55 from $1.65 per share.

But most analysts concentrated on the effectiveness of new packaging innovations and aggessive marketing campaigns in generating business in the United States and other major markets. Much of the added U.S. volume came from the convenience category of sales.
"The company's gaining market share in almost every single soft-drink market in the world," said Roy Burry, an analyst at Oppenheimer & Co.
